claims: H2 'The 1 July 2027 Boost: $37,000 to $45,000, $500 to $810' and the list item 'a full-time worker on $45,000 gets the maximum'
whys: The heading (line 101) and the list item on line 107 type in $37,000, $45,000, $500 and $810 by hand. The body text around them uses NOW.incomeThreshold, NEXT.incomeThreshold, NOW.maxPayment and NEXT.maxPayment. The figures match today, but they will drift if the constants change. Constants: LISTO_CURRENT and LISTO_2027_28 in lib/constants/listo.ts.

claims: Medicare levy phases in at 10c per $1 above $28,011 ... LITO withdrawn at 5c per $1 from $37,500 to $45,000 and 1.5c per $1 from $45,000 to $66,667
whys: The figures are correct today, but they are typed into the FAQ strings (and so into the JSON-LD) instead of coming from constants. They will drift when the ATO publishes the 2026-27 levy thresholds. The same applies to $105,000 at line 35 and to the scale at line 11.

claims: Moving into a higher bracket ... so a raise always increases take-home pay.
whys: The claim is true for brackets but wrong for the Medicare levy surcharge cliff at $105,001 (whole income, no private hospital cover). The answer names the surcharge only as something that makes a raise 'feel small'. The FAQ also feeds FAQPage JSON-LD.

claims: a raise never lowers your take-home pay
whys: The Medicare levy surcharge is charged on the whole income from $105,001 for a single without private hospital cover (line 135 of the same page says so). A $1 raise from $105,000 to $105,001 adds about $1,050 of surcharge, so take-home pay falls. The claim holds only with private hospital cover. The same claim appears in the FAQ (see next item).
reviewerNotes: The writer's Medicare levy surcharge cliff question is valid. 'A raise never lowers your take-home pay' (tsx:58) and 'a raise always increases take-home pay' (faqs.ts:19) are both wrong for a single without private hospital cover who crosses $105,000. The writer correctly left them unchanged. They are for the owner to decide. The writer's average-rate question is a false alarm: the tax on $90,000 is $17,520, plus $1,800 Medicare, which is $19,320, or 21.47%. That correctly rounds to 'about 21%'. On $100,000 the rate is 22.52%, so 'around 22%' is also correct.

claims: The Medicare levy starts at ${LOWER} of taxable income for most people.
whys: The checker flags 'most people' as a population claim. The wording is unchanged from the original. In context it means 'unless you are entitled to SAPTO'. Saying that directly would be more exact than 'for most people'. Please confirm, or reword in a later pass.

claims: The surcharge ... isn't withheld from your pay. The ATO adds it when you lodge.
The Medicare levy is paid by almost every resident
whys: It is not withheld by default. But the ATO's Medicare levy variation declaration (NAT 0929) has a Medicare levy surcharge part that lets an employee ask the employer to withhold extra for the MLS. Saying it 'isn't withheld' is too absolute. Suggested wording: 'isn't withheld unless you ask your employer to'.
This is a population claim with no figure or source. Low-income earners below the Medicare levy threshold and exempt groups do not pay the levy.

reviewerNotes: I agree with the writer's fact questions and pass them on: (1) 'isn't withheld from your pay' is too absolute, because the NAT 0929 Medicare levy variation declaration lets an employee ask for extra withholding for the MLS; (2) 'paid by almost every resident' is a population claim with no source (see the line 201 entries in extraFactQuestions); (3) 'Foster children don't count' (line 194) needs checking against ATO_FAMILY.
